\chapter{What I Know and What I Want}
\label{ch:hi-chaah}
\hlchaptermodality{103}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I know something rather than only that I do not, ask somebody whether they know, and ask for a thing at a counter.}

Answer the counter question aapko kyaa chaahiye with mujhe chaay chaahiye, and say which of the three words carries the information.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maiṁ jāntā hūṁ]{\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ} — the half that was missing}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-jaanta-hun}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I do not know} — you have had that sentence since the chapter on \textbf{\hi{नहीं}}. Now try to say the opposite of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{जानता}}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ।}} — I know.

Nothing about that is new except the permission.

\begin{cousinweb}
You have been saying \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{नहीं} \hi{जानता}} for a very long time. The negative lesson used it as its example sentence, and everything in it was explained except the last word.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you had} & \textbf{what you have now} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} \hi{नहीं} \hi{जानता} & \hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Take \textbf{\hi{नहीं}} out and one thing has to come back: \textbf{\hi{हूँ}}. A Hindi present needs its \emph{to be} on the end, and the negative sentence dropped it — which is ordinary and which is why the affirmative does not look like the negative with a word removed.

The verb is \textbf{\hi{जानना}}, and its \textbf{\hi{ज}} is the letter drawn two chapters before this one. It was on the page long before that, inside \textbf{\hi{जी}} and \textbf{\hi{आज}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a word carried and never handed over}]
This is worth naming because it is a real gap and not a quirk of your memory. The negative lesson's \textbf{headword} names \emph{jāntā} and glosses it as the masculine present of \emph{to know} — but everything that lesson actually teaches is about \textbf{\hi{नहीं}}: its Sanskrit root, its Indo-European cousins, its two jobs.

\textbf{The word rode along in an example and was never handed over.} You could deny knowing something and not claim it, which is a strange shape for a vocabulary to have.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{नहीं} \hi{जानता}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which word comes back when the negative goes away
  \item the infinitive this form is built from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{I know}? (\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ}}.) What did the negative version leave off? (\textbf{\hi{हूँ}}.) Which half of this verb did you have first? (The denial.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyā āp jānte haiṁ?]{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}? — asking it}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-jaante-hain}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I know}. Then say the little word that turns a Hindi statement into a yes-or-no question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}}
\textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}?} — Do you know?

\begin{cousinweb}
Every piece is old and the assembly is regular:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
\hi{क्या} & marks the whole thing as a question \\
\hi{आप} & the respectful \emph{you} \\
\hi{जानते} & the verb, agreeing with \textbf{\hi{आप}} \\
\hi{हैं} & \emph{to be}, also agreeing with \textbf{\hi{आप}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{आप} is grammatically plural}, which is why both the verb and \emph{to be} take their plural endings even when you are speaking to one person. That is not a new rule — it is the same respect-as-plural the track has used since the second chapter, turning up on a new verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where \hi{क्या} sits}]
\textbf{\hi{क्या}} goes at the \textbf{front}, and the rest of the sentence keeps its ordinary order behind it. English reshuffles a question — \emph{you know} becomes \emph{do you know} — and Hindi does not move anything at all.

So a yes-or-no question costs \textbf{one word and no rearrangement}, which makes it one of the cheapest things in the language to build once you can say the statement.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{} — the answer
  \item why the verb is \textbf{\hi{जानते}} and not \textbf{\hi{जानता}}
  \item where \textbf{\hi{क्या}} stands in the sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What turns a statement into a yes-or-no question? (\textbf{\hi{क्या}}, at the front.) Does anything else move? (No.) Why is \textbf{\hi{आप}} followed by plural endings? (It is grammatically plural, however many people you mean.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cāhiye]{\hi{चाहिए} — wanting a thing rather than an action}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-chahiye}



\begin{quote}
Say the verb for wanting, the one you met with \textbf{\hi{सकना}}. Then try to use it to want a \textbf{cup of tea} rather than to want to \emph{do} something.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चाहिए}}
\textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} — \emph{is wanted, is needed}.

It is built from the same root as \textbf{\hi{चाहना}}, and it does a job that verb cannot.

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{what follows it} \\
\midrule
\hi{चाहता} / \hi{चाहती} & another \textbf{verb} \\
\hi{चाहिए} & a \textbf{thing} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{चाहना}} wants an action. It was taught alongside the rule that a Hindi verb can swallow another verb whole, and that is exactly what it does: \emph{I want \textbf{to go}}.

\textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} wants a noun. \emph{I want \textbf{tea}}. English uses one word for both jobs and hides the difference; Hindi uses two forms and makes it visible.

The other difference is that \textbf{\hi{चाहिए} does not change}. It has no masculine and feminine, no singular and plural — the same five letters whoever is speaking and whatever is wanted. After a chapter of endings that agree with everything in sight, that is a relief worth noticing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \hi{ए} on the end}]
The word ends in \textbf{\hi{ए}}, the standing vowel drawn a few chapters back — not the sitting mark \textbf{\hi{◌े}}, because there is no consonant after \textbf{\hi{हि}} for the vowel to ride on.

That is the rule from the letter lesson doing its first real work: \textbf{which of the two shapes a word uses is decided by whether a consonant is there to carry the vowel}, and a word ending in a vowel sound has nothing behind it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{चाहिए}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of the two forms takes a thing after it
  \item which takes an action after it
  \item why the last letter is the standing \textbf{\hi{ए}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} take after it? (A thing.) What does \textbf{\hi{चाहता}} take? (Another verb.) Does \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} change for gender or number? (No — never.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mujhe cāy cāhiye]{\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए} — the wanter is not the subject}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-mujhe-chahiye}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I like tea} in Hindi. Look at the first word you said, and keep it in mind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मुझे} … \hi{चाहिए}}
\textbf{\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए।}} — I want tea.

Not \textbf{\hi{मैं}}. \textbf{\hi{मुझे}} — \emph{to me}.

\subsection*{The two words}
This is the liking sentence again, with one word swapped:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{word for word} \\
\midrule
\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{पसंद} \hi{है} & to me, tea is pleasing \\
\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए} & to me, tea is wanted \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The person is in the dative both times}, and the thing is what the sentence is really about. Hindi treats wanting and liking as things that \textbf{happen to} you rather than things you \textbf{do}, and puts the person on the receiving end of both.

That is not a Hindi peculiarity. The proxy language reaches the same shape in \emph{me gusta}, and Italian in \emph{mi piace} — three languages in two unrelated families building the same idea the same way. What makes Hindi's version worth a lesson is that \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} extends it to \textbf{wanting}, where those languages switch back to an ordinary verb.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what agrees with what}]
\textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} does not change, so there is nothing to agree. The sentence has no word that bends, which is unusual enough to be a useful landmark: \textbf{if you hear \hi{चाहिए}, stop looking for agreement.}

And \textbf{\hi{मुझे}} carries \textbf{\hi{झ}}, the breathy partner drawn a few chapters back. It was in your mouth from the liking chapter onwards and only recently on your hand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{पसंद} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which word is \textbf{not} \textbf{\hi{मैं}}, and why
  \item what in the sentence agrees with anything (nothing)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{I want tea}? (\textbf{\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए}}.) Which case is the wanter in? (The dative — \emph{to me}.) Which other sentence you know puts the person there? (The liking one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cāh kī tālikā]{cāh kī tālikā — wanting, on one page}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-repaso-chaah}



\begin{quote}
Name the two forms of the wanting verb, and say what each one wants after it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one root, two forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{what follows} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\hi{चाहता} / \hi{चाहती} & a \textbf{verb} & \hi{मैं} \hi{जाना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ} \\
\hi{चाहिए} & a \textbf{thing} & \hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Ask what comes next, not what it means.} Both translate into English as \emph{want}, so the meaning will not tell the two apart — the shape of what follows will, every time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: who sits where}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sentence} & \textbf{the person is} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} \hi{जाना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ} & \textbf{\hi{मैं}} — the subject \\
\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए} & \textbf{\hi{मुझे}} — the dative \\
\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{पसंद} \hi{है} & \textbf{\hi{मुझे}} — the dative \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the three put the person on the receiving end, and the one that does not is the one where the person is genuinely doing something — going. \textbf{Wanting a thing and liking a thing happen to you; wanting to act is something you do}, and Hindi draws that line with the case of the first word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb that was only ever denied}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you can now say} & \textbf{what you had before} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ} & only \hi{मैं} \hi{नहीं} \hi{जानता} \\
\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}? & nothing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The affirmative needed no new grammar at all — it needed somebody to introduce the word, which the negative lesson used and never taught.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{जानता} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the question that tells the two wanting forms apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which wanting form takes a noun? (\textbf{\hi{चाहिए}}.) Which case is its wanter in? (The dative.) Does \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} ever bend? (No.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āpko kyā cāhiye?]{\hi{आपको} \hi{क्या} \hi{चाहिए}? — answering at a counter}

\label{lesson:HI-C95-sintesis-chaay}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to you} in its respectful form, and the word that marks a question. Both have been yours for a while.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{speaker} & \textbf{Hindi} \\
\midrule
A & \hi{आपको} \hi{क्या} \hi{चाहिए}? \\
B & \hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The two lines are the \textbf{same sentence with the person swapped} — \textbf{\hi{आपको}} for \textbf{\hi{मुझे}} — and \textbf{\hi{क्या}} standing where the answer will go.

\subsection*{How to answer}
A listening item built on this keys on \textbf{the noun between the two fixed words}. Everything else in B's reply is predictable:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item The first word is the \textbf{dative person} — it tells you who, not what.
  \item The last word is \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} — it never changes, so it carries no information.
  \item \textbf{The answer is whatever sits between them.}
\end{enumerate}

That is why the item is answerable even if the middle word is the only one you catch. Listen to the middle.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the chapter in one sentence}]
Hindi puts the person on the \textbf{receiving end} of wanting, and gives the wanting word \textbf{no endings at all} — so the sentence's whole meaning lives in the noun in the middle and the case of the word in front.

\textbf{\hi{क्या} \hi{आप} \hi{जानते} \hi{हैं}?} works the other way round: there the endings do all the agreeing, because somebody is genuinely doing the knowing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{आपको} \hi{क्या} \hi{चाहिए}?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मुझे} \hi{चाय} \hi{चाहिए}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which word in the answer carries the information
  \item what changed between the question and the answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where in the answer is the information? (The noun in the middle.) What does \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} tell you? (Nothing — it never changes.) What replaces \textbf{\hi{क्या}} when the question is answered? (The thing wanted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
